_metadata.note: The supplied component list contains 51 named items. Every requested item is included. Throughput, latency, and cost values are indicative planning ranges, not provider guarantees. Validate current pricing and benchmark with the real workload before making capacity decisions.

components.name: Load Balancer
components.tagline: Distributes traffic across healthy service instances
components.whatItDoes: A load balancer accepts client connections and routes each request or connection to one of several backends. Layer 4 balancers make decisions using transport information, while Layer 7 balancers can route by host, path, headers, or cookies. Health checks and connection draining keep failed or terminating instances out of rotation.
whenToUse: Failing traffic away from unhealthy instances
Routing requests by hostname, path, region, or service version
whenNotToUse: As a substitute for database sharding
When a single local process is sufficient and high availability is not required

realWorldUsage.useCase: Routes edge and API traffic across service capacity
Uses load balancing as part of a horizontally scaled commerce platform

keyMetrics.throughput: 10K-1M+ requests/sec depending on appliance and payload
keyMetrics.latency: Typically sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds added hop latency
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Indicative managed-cloud starting cost: tens of USD/month plus usage

commonMistakes: Using only shallow TCP checks for an application that is unhealthy at the HTTP layer
Keeping user session state only in local memory without stickiness or shared storage
Ignoring connection draining during deployments
components.interviewTips: Explain Layer 4 versus Layer 7, health checks, least-connections versus round-robin, TLS termination, sticky sessions, and why the database may still become the bottleneck.

components.name: API Gateway
components.tagline: Central entry point for API routing, policy enforcement, and governance
components.whatItDoes: An API gateway sits in front of backend services and provides a stable client-facing API surface. It commonly handles routing, authentication integration, quotas, request validation, transformations, logging, and versioning. A gateway is a policy boundary, not a place to hide all business logic.
whenToUse: Exposing multiple microservices behind one public endpoint
Applying authentication, quotas, and API analytics consistently
Supporting REST, HTTP, or WebSocket APIs for external consumers
whenNotToUse: Putting complex domain workflows into gateway scripts
Adding a gateway to a small internal service where a reverse proxy is enough

realWorldUsage.useCase: API Gateway exposes REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at scale
Uses edge services to centralize cross-cutting concerns before internal services

keyMetrics.throughput: Provider quotas vary; design for burst and steady-state limits
keyMetrics.latency: Usually adds a few to tens of milliseconds depending on features
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usually usage based; validate current provider pricing

commonMistakes: Treating throttling targets as hard guarantees
Building a single oversized gateway configuration owned by nobody
Failing to propagate correlation IDs and client identity downstream
components.interviewTips: Differentiate an API gateway from a reverse proxy and load balancer. Discuss authentication, throttling, observability, request validation, and avoiding a gateway monolith.

components.name: CDN
components.tagline: Caches and serves content close to users at the network edge
components.whatItDoes: A content delivery network places cache nodes near users so static files and cacheable responses travel a shorter network path. CDNs reduce origin load, improve latency, and absorb large traffic bursts. Modern CDNs can also terminate TLS, apply edge rules, and protect origins.
whenToUse: Serving images, JavaScript, CSS, downloads, and video segments
Reducing global latency for cacheable content
whenNotToUse: Serving highly personalized responses without a deliberate cache-key strategy
Assuming cached data is instantly invalidated everywhere

realWorldUsage.useCase: Open Connect localizes playable content near viewers inside ISP and interconnection networks
Provides globally distributed edge caching and security services

keyMetrics.throughput: Designed for internet-scale delivery; capacity depends on provider and cache hit ratio
keyMetrics.latency: Often tens of milliseconds saved by avoiding distant origin trips
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based by data transfer and requests

commonMistakes: Caching private content under a shared key
Using very long TTLs without versioned asset URLs or purge strategy
Ignoring origin shielding and cache stampede protection
components.interviewTips: Discuss cache keys, TTLs, invalidation, hit ratio, origin shielding, signed URLs, and why video delivery differs from API response caching.

components.name: WAF
components.tagline: Filters malicious HTTP requests before they reach applications
components.whatItDoes: A web application firewall inspects HTTP traffic and applies managed or custom rules. It can block common attack patterns, suspicious bots, abusive IPs, and malformed requests. It complements secure coding; it cannot repair insecure authorization logic inside the application.
whenToUse: Applying bot controls and IP reputation checks
Adding virtual patches while application fixes are deployed
whenNotToUse: Replacing input validation and authorization checks
Protecting non-HTTP protocols without an appropriate network firewall

realWorldUsage.useCase: AWS WAF integrates with edge and API services
Provides managed WAF rules and bot controls at the edge

keyMetrics.throughput: Scales with edge or gateway service capacity
keyMetrics.latency: Usually low single-digit millisecond overhead for typical rule sets
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based on requests and enabled rules

commonMistakes: Enabling blocking mode before testing false positives
Using generic rules without application-specific allowlists and rate rules
Not monitoring rule matches after deployment
components.interviewTips: State that WAF is defense in depth. Describe managed rules, custom rules, false positives, logging, rate-based rules, and the limits of signature matching.

components.name: DNS
components.tagline: Translates service names into routable endpoints
components.whatItDoes: The Domain Name System maps human-friendly names to IP addresses or other records. Recursive resolvers cache answers based on TTL, while authoritative servers publish the source records. DNS is also used for traffic steering, failover, service discovery, and verification records.
whenToUse: Mapping public domains to edge endpoints
Internal service discovery where DNS semantics are sufficient
whenNotToUse: Requiring instant global failover without respecting resolver caching
Storing rapidly changing application state in DNS

realWorldUsage.useCase: Operates public DNS resolver infrastructure
Route 53 supports DNS routing and health-check-based failover

keyMetrics.throughput: Authoritative services are designed for very high query volume
keyMetrics.latency: Cached lookups are often single-digit milliseconds; uncached resolution may be slower
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usually low per-zone and per-query charges

commonMistakes: Choosing a long TTL for a record that needs fast failover
Forgetting negative caching and resolver behavior
Creating a circular dependency where recovery tools depend on the failed DNS path
components.interviewTips: Cover recursive versus authoritative DNS, TTL trade-offs, A/AAAA/CNAME records, health checks, propagation myths, and why DNS failures can be system-wide.

components.name: Reverse Proxy
components.tagline: Receives client traffic and forwards it to internal servers
components.whatItDoes: A reverse proxy hides backend topology behind a stable endpoint. It can terminate TLS, route requests, compress responses, add headers, cache selected content, and enforce simple policies. Unlike a forward proxy, it represents servers to clients rather than clients to external servers.
whenToUse: Routing multiple applications behind one public endpoint
Adding compression, caching, or header normalization
whenNotToUse: Implementing complex authorization solely through proxy configuration
Assuming a single proxy instance is highly available

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses proxy layers to front web application services
Has publicly discussed load balancers and proxy systems at its perimeter

keyMetrics.throughput: Thousands to hundreds of thousands of requests/sec per tuned instance
keyMetrics.latency: Often sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds added overhead
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Open-source software cost is zero; infrastructure cost varies

commonMistakes: Running only one proxy instance
Forwarding untrusted client headers without normalization
Missing timeout alignment between proxy and upstream
components.interviewTips: Contrast reverse proxy, load balancer, and API gateway. Mention TLS termination, upstream pools, buffering, timeouts, header trust, and high availability.

components.name: Rate Limiter
components.tagline: Controls request volume to protect capacity and enforce fairness
components.whatItDoes: A rate limiter decides whether a request should proceed based on a policy such as requests per second, concurrency, or cost units. Common algorithms include token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, and sliding window. Distributed limits require careful consistency and failure-mode choices.
whenToUse: Enforcing tenant quotas and plan limits
Preventing brute-force login attempts and abusive scraping
whenNotToUse: Using one global limit that penalizes every tenant equally
Relying on rate limiting as the only DDoS control

realWorldUsage.useCase: Publishes API rate limits for client fairness
API Gateway supports throttling and quotas

keyMetrics.throughput: Often 10K-1M decisions/sec depending on local or distributed implementation
keyMetrics.latency: Target sub-millisecond for local or Redis-backed checks
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usually embedded in gateway or backed by a small cache cluster

commonMistakes: Not returning retry guidance such as Retry-After
Ignoring burst capacity and only configuring average rate
Failing open or closed without an explicit policy when the limiter store is unavailable
components.interviewTips: Explain token bucket, per-user versus global limits, distributed counters, hot keys, fail-open versus fail-closed behavior, and 429 responses.

components.name: Microservice
components.tagline: Small independently deployable service around a bounded capability
components.whatItDoes: A microservice owns a focused business capability and exposes a contract through an API or events. The architectural benefit is independent evolution and scaling, but the cost is distributed failure modes, operational overhead, and data consistency complexity. A service boundary should follow ownership and domain behavior rather than arbitrary code size.
whenToUse: Separating domains with different ownership or scaling needs
Isolating workloads with distinct reliability requirements
whenNotToUse: Splitting a small product into dozens of services prematurely
Sharing one database schema across services while pretending they are independent

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses a large service-oriented architecture for streaming and product capabilities
Operates many backend components supported by internal platform tooling

keyMetrics.throughput: Depends on implementation and downstreams
keyMetrics.latency: Each network hop may add milliseconds and failure risk
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Operational cost grows with service count and platform maturity needs

commonMistakes: Nano-services that add hops without autonomy
Synchronous call chains with no timeout budgets
Unclear data ownership
components.interviewTips: Discuss bounded contexts, team ownership, data ownership, service contracts, observability, retries, and why a modular monolith is often the correct starting point.

components.name: Serverless Function (Lambda)
components.tagline: Event-driven compute that scales without managing servers
components.whatItDoes: A serverless function runs code in response to an event or request while the cloud provider manages provisioning and scaling. It is useful for bursty, short-lived workloads and glue logic. Constraints such as cold starts, execution duration, concurrency quotas, and statelessness shape the design.
whenToUse: Handling bursty APIs with low idle traffic
whenNotToUse: Long-running compute-intensive processes without a suitable runtime model
Latency-critical paths where cold starts are unacceptable without mitigation

realWorldUsage.useCase: AWS has described Netflix using Lambda for self-managing infrastructure
AWS describes a Lambda-based workload for analyzing large volumes of market events

keyMetrics.throughput: Scales with concurrency quotas and downstream capacity
keyMetrics.latency: Warm invocations can be low-latency; cold starts vary by runtime and package
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based on requests and execution duration

commonMistakes: Ignoring downstream database connection limits during rapid scale-out
Packaging oversized dependencies that increase cold-start time
Assuming exactly-once event processing
components.interviewTips: Mention cold starts, idempotency, concurrency controls, event retries, dead-letter handling, observability, and when containers are a better fit.

components.name: Docker Container
components.tagline: Portable process package with isolated filesystem and dependencies
components.whatItDoes: A container image packages application code, runtime libraries, and configuration defaults into an immutable artifact. Containers share the host kernel, making them lighter than virtual machines. The image improves repeatability, but production safety still depends on runtime limits, scanning, secrets, and orchestration.
whenToUse: Running isolated workloads on shared hosts
whenNotToUse: Treating containers as a security boundary equivalent to separate physical machines
Baking secrets into images

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses containerized platform practices including Kubernetes adoption
Uses containerized and service-oriented workloads for selected systems

keyMetrics.throughput: Application dependent
keyMetrics.latency: Near-native runtime performance for most workloads
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Docker tooling is available freely; compute cost depends on runtime platform

commonMistakes: Using mutable latest tags in production
Running as root unnecessarily
Not setting CPU and memory limits
components.interviewTips: Explain images versus containers, layers, registries, immutable tags, health checks, resource limits, non-root users, and the difference between Docker and Kubernetes.

components.name: Kubernetes Pod
components.tagline: Smallest deployable Kubernetes unit containing one or more containers
components.whatItDoes: A Kubernetes Pod groups one or more cooperating containers that are scheduled together and share networking and selected resources. Most application Pods contain one main container plus optional sidecars. Pods are disposable; controllers create replacements when instances fail or deployments change.
whenToUse: Running application containers under Kubernetes controllers
Co-locating a sidecar that must share lifecycle or network namespace
Defining readiness, liveness, and resource requests for a workload
whenNotToUse: Persisting important data only inside the Pod filesystem
Manually treating individual Pod IPs as durable endpoints

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has publicly discussed adopting Kubernetes in its supported engineering path
Pods are the fundamental workload unit across Kubernetes deployments

keyMetrics.throughput: Application dependent
keyMetrics.latency: Application dependent; scheduling and startup affect recovery time
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Kubernetes software is open source; cluster and compute costs vary

commonMistakes: Confusing liveness with readiness checks
Omitting resource requests and limits
Depending on a Pod identity that disappears during rescheduling
components.interviewTips: Explain shared network namespace, controllers, readiness versus liveness, resource requests and limits, ephemeral lifecycle, and sidecars.

components.name: Auto Scaler
components.tagline: Adjusts capacity as demand changes
components.whatItDoes: An auto scaler increases or decreases capacity based on observed metrics or forecasts. Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling changes resources assigned to an instance. Good scaling policies account for warm-up time, downstream bottlenecks, cooldown windows, and the fact that scaling is not instantaneous.
whenToUse: Handling predictable and unpredictable traffic variation
Maintaining target utilization or queue depth
whenNotToUse: Masking memory leaks or inefficient queries instead of fixing them
Scaling stateless workers without checking downstream quotas

realWorldUsage.useCase: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes workload capacity to match demand
EC2 Auto Scaling adjusts fleet capacity based on policies

keyMetrics.throughput: Capacity increases with instances until a shared bottleneck is reached
keyMetrics.latency: Scale-out reaction ranges from seconds to minutes
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Can lower idle cost but may increase spend during spikes

commonMistakes: Scaling only on CPU when queue depth or latency is the real signal
No maximum capacity guardrail
Aggressive scale-in that removes warm capacity too early
components.interviewTips: Discuss horizontal versus vertical scaling, metrics, cooldowns, predictive scaling, queue-based workers, and why databases often constrain linear scaling.

components.name: PostgreSQL
components.tagline: Relational database for transactional integrity and rich SQL
components.whatItDoes: PostgreSQL stores structured data in tables with constraints, indexes, transactions, and a powerful SQL engine. It is a strong default for systems that need correctness, joins, and evolving query patterns. Scaling reads is straightforward with replicas; scaling writes may require partitioning, sharding, or architectural changes.
whenToUse: Systems needing ACID transactions and strong constraints
whenNotToUse: Massive write scale that cannot be handled by one primary without a sharding plan
Unstructured blob storage

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has publicly discussed operating PostgreSQL at large scale
Uses PostgreSQL for core application data

keyMetrics.throughput: Thousands to tens of thousands of transactions/sec per tuned primary depending on workload
keyMetrics.latency: Single-digit milliseconds is common for indexed queries near the database
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed starter instances often begin at tens of USD/month

commonMistakes: Missing indexes on frequent filters and joins
Long transactions that hold locks and delay vacuum
Opening unbounded connections instead of pooling
components.interviewTips: Cover ACID, MVCC, indexes, query plans, replicas, partitioning, connection pooling, vacuum, and the point at which sharding becomes necessary.

components.name: MySQL
components.tagline: Widely used relational database for reliable OLTP workloads
components.whatItDoes: MySQL is a relational database commonly used for web and transactional applications. It offers indexes, transactions, replication, and a mature operational ecosystem. The design discussion is less about brand preference and more about schema quality, access patterns, failover, and write-scaling limits.
whenToUse: Teams needing a mature relational database ecosystem
whenNotToUse: Analytical scans that belong in a warehouse
Storing large media objects directly in database rows without a reason

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has publicly discussed MySQL infrastructure and failover incidents
Has published engineering work involving MySQL-based storage systems

keyMetrics.throughput: Thousands to tens of thousands of transactions/sec depending on workload
keyMetrics.latency: Often low milliseconds for indexed point queries
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed starter instances often begin at tens of USD/month

commonMistakes: Assuming replicas are immediately consistent
Relying on implicit schema behavior rather than explicit constraints
Ignoring slow query logs and execution plans
components.interviewTips: Explain primary-replica topology, indexes, transactions, replication lag, failover, schema migrations, and when to introduce cache or sharding.

components.name: MongoDB
components.tagline: Document database for flexible JSON-like records and horizontal scale
components.whatItDoes: MongoDB stores BSON documents grouped into collections. It supports indexes, replication through replica sets, and horizontal partitioning through sharding. It fits aggregate-shaped data well, but flexible schema is not a license to ignore validation, query planning, or document growth.
whenToUse: Rapidly evolving aggregates with nested fields
Horizontal scale where shard-key design is understood
whenNotToUse: Highly relational workloads dominated by multi-entity joins
Using an ever-growing document as an unbounded event log

realWorldUsage.useCase: Used for document-oriented operational workloads across many industries
MongoDB has published customer stories involving application data platforms

keyMetrics.throughput: Thousands to hundreds of thousands of ops/sec depending on cluster and access pattern
keyMetrics.latency: Often low milliseconds for indexed operations
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed development tiers may be free or low-cost; production cost varies by cluster

commonMistakes: Selecting a low-cardinality or monotonically hot shard key
Skipping schema validation completely
Creating too many indexes and slowing writes
components.interviewTips: Cover document modeling, embedding versus referencing, indexes, replica sets, shard keys, balancing, write concern, read concern, and transactions.

components.name: Redis
components.tagline: In-memory data store for low-latency access
components.whatItDoes: Redis stores data structures such as strings, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, and probabilistic structures primarily in memory. It is commonly used as a cache, rate-limiter backend, session store, leaderboard, or lightweight coordination tool. Persistence and clustering options exist, but memory economics and failure semantics must be explicit.
whenToUse: Rate limiting, sessions, counters, and leaderboards
Fast ephemeral coordination and stream processing
whenNotToUse: Using Redis as the only durable store for irreplaceable data without a persistence and recovery plan
Caching large low-value objects that exceed memory economics

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has publicly described Redis use for rate limiting and caching patterns
Has historically discussed timeline and cache-heavy architectures

keyMetrics.throughput: 100K-1M+ ops/sec depending on command mix, pipelining, and topology
keyMetrics.latency: Common target below 1ms on a healthy local network path
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed small-node starting cost is often tens of USD/month

commonMistakes: No TTL policy for cache keys
Using expensive commands on large collections in the request path
Allowing a cache stampede after expiry
components.interviewTips: Discuss data structures, TTLs, eviction, persistence, replication, cluster hash slots, pipelining, hot keys, cache stampedes, and why benchmarks depend on workload.

components.name: Cassandra
components.tagline: Wide-column database optimized for scalable writes and high availability
components.whatItDoes: Apache Cassandra distributes partitioned data across a cluster with replication and tunable consistency. It is well suited to large write-heavy workloads with known query patterns and no single primary. Data modeling starts from queries because joins and ad hoc relational access are limited.
whenToUse: Workloads that can model queries around partition keys
whenNotToUse: Applications requiring rich joins and ad hoc SQL analytics
Using unbounded partitions that become operationally expensive

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has publicly described Cassandra in multiple platform systems
Has published engineering work on storing large volumes of message data using Cassandra and later alternatives

keyMetrics.throughput: Scales horizontally with nodes for suitable workloads
keyMetrics.latency: Often single-digit to tens of milliseconds depending on consistency and topology
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Infrastructure cost depends on node count, storage, and replication factor

commonMistakes: Unbounded partitions
Choosing consistency levels without understanding quorum behavior
Treating Cassandra like a relational database
components.interviewTips: Explain partition keys, clustering columns, replication factor, consistency levels, compaction, tombstones, repair, and query-first modeling.

components.name: Elasticsearch
components.tagline: Distributed search engine for full-text retrieval and analytics
components.whatItDoes: Elasticsearch indexes documents into inverted indexes so text search, filtering, and aggregations are fast. Shards distribute data and replicas add read capacity and resilience. It is usually a secondary search index fed from a source of truth, not the only system of record.
whenNotToUse: Primary transactional storage for critical business records
High-frequency updates to deeply nested documents without modeling care

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses search indexing for code and issue discovery
Use Elasticsearch for search, observability, and security analytics

keyMetrics.throughput: Varies widely with shard count, indexing rate, query complexity, and hardware
keyMetrics.latency: Common search targets are tens to hundreds of milliseconds
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed clusters commonly start at tens to hundreds of USD/month

commonMistakes: Too many tiny shards
Mapping explosions from uncontrolled dynamic fields
Expecting immediate consistency after indexing
components.interviewTips: Discuss inverted indexes, analyzers, mappings, shards, replicas, refresh interval, eventual visibility, reindexing, and source-of-truth separation.

components.name: DynamoDB
components.tagline: Managed key-value and document database with predictable scale
components.whatItDoes: Amazon DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database designed around partition keys, optional sort keys, and access-pattern-first modeling. It automatically distributes data, but hot partitions and inefficient scans still matter. Secondary indexes, streams, conditional writes, and TTLs support common application patterns.
whenToUse: Serverless applications with known access patterns
Workloads needing managed scaling and low operational overhead
whenNotToUse: Relational joins and exploratory queries
Using table scans as the normal request path

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use DynamoDB for serverless and internet-scale operational workloads
Dynamo-style design principles originated from Amazon's availability needs

keyMetrics.throughput: Scales to very high request rates when keys distribute traffic well
keyMetrics.latency: Single-digit millisecond design target for many operations
keyMetrics.typicalCost: On-demand or provisioned usage pricing; validate current rates

commonMistakes: Hot partition keys
Overusing scans
Designing the schema before listing access patterns
components.interviewTips: Explain partition keys, sort keys, GSIs, LSIs, hot partitions, conditional writes, streams, TTL, provisioned versus on-demand capacity, and single-table design trade-offs.

components.name: Object Storage (S3)
components.tagline: Durable object storage for files, backups, and data lakes
components.whatItDoes: Object storage stores blobs under keys inside buckets rather than rows or filesystem blocks. Amazon S3 is a common example: applications use it for media, backups, static assets, logs, and analytical data. Object storage is durable and scalable but has different access semantics from a database or mounted disk.
whenToUse: Backups, archives, logs, and data lake objects
Static website assets and origin storage for a CDN
whenNotToUse: Low-latency row-level transactional updates
Using object listing as a high-frequency database query

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses cloud object storage as part of large-scale media and data workflows
Uses object-oriented storage concepts for file content at scale

keyMetrics.throughput: Scales horizontally; request patterns and prefixes should still be designed sensibly
keyMetrics.latency: Typically tens to hundreds of milliseconds per request
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based on stored GB, requests, retrieval, and transfer

commonMistakes: Public bucket exposure
No lifecycle policy for old data
Assuming a successful upload automatically means application metadata is consistent
components.interviewTips: Compare object storage with block storage and databases. Discuss presigned URLs, multipart uploads, lifecycle tiers, versioning, encryption, access policies, and CDN integration.

components.name: Data Warehouse
components.tagline: Analytical store optimized for scans, aggregations, and business reporting
components.whatItDoes: A data warehouse centralizes historical data for analytical queries. Columnar storage, partition pruning, compression, and distributed execution make large scans efficient. Warehouses should be fed through controlled pipelines so analysts can trust definitions, lineage, and freshness.
whenToUse: Batch and interactive analytical queries over large datasets
whenNotToUse: Serving transactional request-path writes
Using raw production tables without governance as the only reporting layer

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has published data platform work supporting analytics and experimentation
Uses large-scale analytics platforms to optimize product and streaming operations

keyMetrics.throughput: Optimized for parallel scans rather than OLTP requests/sec
keyMetrics.latency: Seconds to minutes for analytical queries depending on size and optimization
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Compute and storage usage based; can range from modest to substantial

commonMistakes: No partitioning or clustering strategy
Duplicated business metrics with inconsistent definitions
Letting unbounded dashboard queries consume all warehouse capacity
components.interviewTips: Explain OLTP versus OLAP, columnar storage, partitions, materialized views, ETL/ELT, dimensional modeling, cost controls, and data freshness.

components.name: Time Series Database
components.tagline: Storage optimized for timestamped measurements and retention policies
components.whatItDoes: A time series database stores values indexed primarily by time and dimensions such as host, service, or sensor. It supports efficient append-heavy writes, range scans, downsampling, retention, and aggregations. It is useful for monitoring and telemetry but can suffer from high-cardinality labels.
whenToUse: Financial or operational measurements over time
whenNotToUse: General relational business data
Unbounded high-cardinality tags without capacity planning

realWorldUsage.useCase: Store and query timestamped monitoring samples
Visualizes time series from many supported backends

keyMetrics.throughput: Often designed for high append rates
keyMetrics.latency: Range queries commonly target milliseconds to seconds
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Depends heavily on retention, sample interval, and cardinality

commonMistakes: High-cardinality label explosions
Keeping raw high-resolution data forever
Using timestamps without a clear retention and rollup policy
components.interviewTips: Discuss append patterns, tags, high cardinality, retention, downsampling, compression, late-arriving data, and why monitoring data needs bounded cost.

components.name: Graph Database
components.tagline: Models relationships as first-class nodes and edges
components.whatItDoes: A graph database stores entities and relationships directly, making multi-hop traversal natural. It fits problems where the path between records matters as much as individual records. Graph systems can simplify recommendation, fraud, and dependency queries, but are not automatically better for ordinary CRUD.
whenNotToUse: Simple key-value lookups
Replacing a relational database without relationship-heavy access patterns

realWorldUsage.useCase: Popularized graph-oriented thinking for professional relationships
Dependency and collaboration relationships are naturally graph-shaped

keyMetrics.throughput: Highly workload dependent; traversal depth and fan-out dominate
keyMetrics.latency: Point lookups can be fast; deep traversals can become expensive
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed graph services often start above simple database starter tiers

commonMistakes: Unbounded traversals
Missing edge direction and relationship semantics
Assuming graph modeling removes the need for indexes
components.interviewTips: Explain nodes, edges, properties, traversal depth, fan-out limits, indexing, graph partitioning difficulty, and when relational tables remain simpler.

components.name: Apache Kafka
components.tagline: Partitioned event log for durable high-throughput streaming
components.whatItDoes: Kafka stores ordered records in partitions and lets consumer groups read at their own pace. Retention allows replay, making Kafka useful as an event backbone and stream-processing source. Ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across an entire topic.
whenToUse: Replayable integration events and analytics feeds
whenNotToUse: Simple low-volume task queues needing per-message routing and easy retries
Assuming global ordering while using many partitions

realWorldUsage.useCase: Created Kafka for event and activity data pipelines
Uses Kafka-style streaming patterns in large-scale data systems

keyMetrics.throughput: Hundreds of thousands to millions of messages/sec per cluster depending on payload and durability
keyMetrics.latency: Often milliseconds to tens of milliseconds
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Managed clusters commonly start at hundreds of USD/month; self-managed cost varies

commonMistakes: Too few partitions for scale or too many for operational simplicity
No idempotency strategy for reprocessing
Ignoring consumer lag
components.interviewTips: Discuss topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, retention, replay, replication, ordering scope, delivery semantics, compaction, and consumer lag.

components.name: RabbitMQ
components.tagline: Message broker for queues, routing, acknowledgements, and work distribution
components.whatItDoes: RabbitMQ accepts messages from publishers, routes them through exchanges, and delivers them from queues to consumers. It supports acknowledgements, publisher confirms, dead-lettering, priorities, and multiple routing styles. It is often a good fit for task distribution and integration workflows.
whenToUse: Routing messages to different consumers using exchanges
Work queues with acknowledgement and retry behavior
whenNotToUse: Very large retained event logs that need replay for months
Using a queue without dead-letter handling for poison messages

realWorldUsage.useCase: Used broadly for application messaging and work queues
Offer managed RabbitMQ-compatible broker services

keyMetrics.throughput: Thousands to hundreds of thousands of messages/sec depending on durability and topology
keyMetrics.latency: Usually milliseconds
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Self-managed or managed broker; small production deployments often tens to hundreds of USD/month

commonMistakes: Auto-ack before processing finishes
Unlimited prefetch that overloads consumers
No dead-letter queue
components.interviewTips: Explain exchanges, queues, bindings, acknowledgements, publisher confirms, durability, prefetch, dead-letter queues, and when Kafka is a better fit.

components.name: Amazon SQS
components.tagline: Managed queue for decoupling producers and workers
components.whatItDoes: Amazon Simple Queue Service stores messages until consumers retrieve and delete them. Visibility timeout prevents immediate redelivery while a worker processes a message. Standard queues prioritize scale and at-least-once delivery; FIFO queues add ordering and deduplication features with different constraints.
whenToUse: Decoupling web requests from background work
whenNotToUse: Requiring complex broker-side routing
Assuming one delivery without idempotent consumers

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use SQS to decouple asynchronous workloads
Commonly pair API Gateway, Lambda, and SQS

keyMetrics.throughput: Very high managed throughput; FIFO and account quotas should be checked
keyMetrics.latency: Typically low tens of milliseconds or more depending on polling
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based per API request

commonMistakes: Visibility timeout shorter than processing duration
Deleting before processing succeeds
No dead-letter queue or redrive policy
components.interviewTips: Discuss standard versus FIFO, visibility timeout, long polling, at-least-once delivery, idempotency, DLQs, redrive, and backpressure.

components.name: Amazon SNS
components.tagline: Managed publish-subscribe fan-out service
components.whatItDoes: Amazon Simple Notification Service publishes a message to a topic and fans it out to subscribed endpoints such as queues, functions, HTTP endpoints, or email. It is useful for broadcasting events to multiple independent consumers. Durable processing is often achieved by subscribing queues rather than relying only on direct delivery.
whenToUse: Fan-out from one event to multiple services
Sending events to multiple SQS queues
whenNotToUse: Storing a replayable event history
Complex stream transformations

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use SNS topics for pub-sub fan-out
Use SNS to trigger multiple downstream workflows

keyMetrics.throughput: Managed scale with service quotas
keyMetrics.latency: Typically near real-time delivery
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based per publish and delivery

commonMistakes: Using direct HTTP delivery without retry and idempotency planning
Assuming subscriber ordering
No subscription filter strategy
components.interviewTips: Compare SNS fan-out with SQS work queues, EventBridge routing, and Kafka logs. Mention retries, DLQs, filtering, ordering expectations, and subscriber independence.

components.name: Amazon EventBridge
components.tagline: Managed event bus for routing events by rules
components.whatItDoes: EventBridge receives events from applications, AWS services, and partner systems, then routes matching events to targets. Rules inspect event structure rather than requiring each producer to know consumers. It is useful for loosely coupled workflows and integrations, but it is not a general replacement for a high-throughput retained stream.
whenNotToUse: Very high-volume retained telemetry streams
Workflows needing strict total ordering

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use EventBridge to route cloud and application events
AWS documents EventBridge rules for reacting to malware-protection scan events

keyMetrics.throughput: Managed service with quotas that should be validated
keyMetrics.latency: Typically near real-time but not a hard real-time guarantee
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based per published, matched, or delivered event depending on feature

commonMistakes: Rules that silently drop unmatched events
No schema ownership
Using an event bus where a queue is needed for worker backpressure
components.interviewTips: Explain event bus, rules, targets, schemas, retries, DLQs, idempotency, and the difference between routing events and buffering work.

components.name: NATS
components.tagline: Lightweight messaging system for low-latency service communication
components.whatItDoes: NATS provides lightweight publish-subscribe and request-reply messaging, with JetStream adding persistence and stream features. Its simple protocol and low overhead suit internal service messaging. The design must distinguish ephemeral core messaging from persisted delivery guarantees.
whenToUse: Edge or distributed messaging with a lightweight broker
whenNotToUse: Assuming persistence when using only ephemeral core NATS
Replacing a durable data pipeline without evaluating retention and replay requirements

realWorldUsage.useCase: Used in cloud-native and edge systems
NATS is used as a messaging component in distributed platforms

keyMetrics.throughput: High message rates with low overhead depending on topology and persistence
keyMetrics.latency: Often sub-millisecond to low milliseconds on local networks
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Open-source software; infrastructure and managed-service cost vary

commonMistakes: Confusing core NATS with JetStream guarantees
No subject naming governance
Ignoring slow consumers
components.interviewTips: Discuss subjects, pub-sub, request-reply, queue groups, JetStream, slow consumers, delivery semantics, and how it differs from Kafka and RabbitMQ.

components.name: Cloud Pub/Sub
components.tagline: Managed asynchronous messaging for event fan-out and streaming ingestion
components.whatItDoes: Cloud Pub/Sub is a managed messaging service that lets publishers send messages to topics and subscribers process them through subscriptions. It decouples services and supports scalable ingestion. Consumers must handle retries, ordering scope, and duplicate delivery according to the selected configuration.
whenNotToUse: Needing relational transactions across message publication and database writes without an outbox pattern
Assuming duplicate-free processing by default

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use Pub/Sub for asynchronous integration and ingestion
Use Pub/Sub as an entry point for stream processing

keyMetrics.throughput: Managed horizontal scale subject to quotas
keyMetrics.latency: Often low milliseconds to seconds depending on delivery mode and load
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usage based on message volume and delivery

commonMistakes: No idempotency keys
Unbounded subscriber backlog
Ignoring ordering-key hotspots
components.interviewTips: Cover topics, subscriptions, push versus pull, acknowledgements, retry, dead-letter handling, ordering keys, backlogs, and idempotent processing.

components.name: Kubernetes Service
components.tagline: Stable virtual endpoint for a changing set of Pods
components.whatItDoes: A Kubernetes Service provides a stable network identity and selects Pods using labels. It decouples clients from disposable Pod IPs and can expose workloads internally or externally. Headless Services intentionally skip a single virtual IP when direct discovery is required.
whenToUse: Discovering Pods behind a stable name
Exposing a workload through ClusterIP, NodePort, or LoadBalancer semantics
whenNotToUse: Addressing individual Pods as if they were permanent
Using a Service alone when HTTP host and path routing are required

realWorldUsage.useCase: Services are the standard abstraction for stable Pod access
Use Services for internal discovery and traffic distribution

keyMetrics.throughput: Depends on implementation and backend capacity
keyMetrics.latency: Low routing overhead in typical cluster networking
keyMetrics.typicalCost: ClusterIP has no direct cloud load-balancer charge; external load balancers may cost extra

commonMistakes: Selector labels do not match intended Pods
Confusing Service readiness with application readiness
Using NodePort publicly without a deliberate security design
components.interviewTips: Explain ClusterIP, LoadBalancer, NodePort, headless Services, selectors, endpoints, and the relationship between Service and Ingress.

components.name: Ingress Controller
components.tagline: Implements external HTTP routing into a Kubernetes cluster
components.whatItDoes: An Ingress resource describes host and path routing rules, while an Ingress controller watches those resources and configures an actual proxy or load balancer. It commonly provides TLS termination and name-based virtual hosting. Gateway API is increasingly relevant for newer Kubernetes traffic-management designs.
whenToUse: Routing multiple HTTP services through one external endpoint
Standardizing web entry into a cluster
whenNotToUse: Non-HTTP protocols without a controller-specific solution
Assuming the Ingress resource works without an installed controller

realWorldUsage.useCase: Ingress controllers implement cluster HTTP entry routing
Offer managed ingress or gateway implementations

keyMetrics.throughput: Depends on controller and underlying load balancer
keyMetrics.latency: Usually low single-digit millisecond proxy overhead
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Controller software may be open source; external load balancer cost varies

commonMistakes: Deploying an Ingress resource but no controller
No TLS automation or certificate monitoring
Treating controller-specific annotations as portable
components.interviewTips: Explain resource versus controller, TLS, path routing, controller-specific behavior, high availability, and when to discuss Gateway API.

components.name: Service Mesh (Istio)
components.tagline: Manages service-to-service traffic, identity, and telemetry
components.whatItDoes: A service mesh adds a data plane and control plane for internal traffic management. It can provide mutual TLS, retries, traffic shifting, policy, and telemetry without every application implementing those features independently. The benefit must justify added complexity and resource overhead.
whenNotToUse: Small systems where library or gateway controls are enough
Using retries blindly and amplifying overload

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use meshes such as Istio for traffic policy and identity
Adopt service meshes when cross-cutting network policy becomes hard to manage

keyMetrics.throughput: Application and proxy dependent
keyMetrics.latency: Adds proxy processing overhead, often measurable in low milliseconds
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Open-source software; operational and compute overhead can be significant

commonMistakes: Enabling every feature at once
Retry policies that cause retry storms
Ignoring sidecar resource consumption
components.interviewTips: Discuss sidecars or ambient approaches, control plane, data plane, mTLS, retries, traffic shifting, observability, and the operational trade-off.

components.name: Config Server
components.tagline: Central source for versioned runtime configuration
components.whatItDoes: A config server stores environment-specific application settings outside deployment artifacts. Services fetch or receive configuration updates while preserving version history and access control. Safe rollout matters because a bad configuration can fail many services faster than a code deployment.
whenToUse: Centralizing feature flags and runtime settings
Separating deployable artifacts from environment configuration
whenNotToUse: Storing secrets without appropriate encryption and access controls
Pushing unvalidated global changes instantly to every instance

realWorldUsage.useCase: Created Archaius-style dynamic configuration patterns for services
Use centralized configuration stores and feature-flag systems

keyMetrics.throughput: Usually modest but availability is critical
keyMetrics.latency: Reads should be cached locally; startup dependency must be resilient
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Often included in platform tooling or backed by a small managed store

commonMistakes: No schema validation
No rollback or version history
Making every request synchronously depend on the config server
components.interviewTips: Explain local caching, versioning, gradual rollout, validation, defaults, fail-safe behavior, audit trails, and separation from secret management.

components.name: Secret Manager
components.tagline: Stores and controls access to credentials and encryption material
components.whatItDoes: A secret manager protects passwords, API keys, certificates, and tokens with encryption, access policies, and audit logs. Applications retrieve secrets at runtime or through controlled injection. Rotation and least privilege reduce the blast radius when a credential is exposed.
whenToUse: Centralized audit of sensitive credential access
whenNotToUse: Committing credentials to source control
Using one shared secret for every environment and service

realWorldUsage.useCase: Offer managed secret stores and key-management integrations
Integrate external secret stores or carefully controlled Secret resources

keyMetrics.throughput: Low to moderate; applications should cache appropriately
keyMetrics.latency: Usually milliseconds to tens of milliseconds; avoid per-request fetches
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Often low usage-based cost plus key-management charges

commonMistakes: Logging secret values
Never rotating credentials
Giving broad read permission to all workloads
components.interviewTips: Cover encryption at rest, transport security, IAM policies, rotation, versioning, audit logs, bootstrap identity, caching, and emergency revocation.

components.name: Cache-Aside
components.tagline: Application loads missing data into cache on demand
components.whatItDoes: With cache-aside, the application checks the cache first, reads the database on a miss, then populates the cache. It is simple and widely used because the cache only contains requested data. The application must manage TTLs, invalidation, and stampede protection.
whenToUse: Optional cache where database remains source of truth
Gradual caching without changing write path
whenNotToUse: Strongly consistent reads immediately after writes without an invalidation strategy
Low-reuse data that wastes cache memory

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use cache-aside for hot database reads
Commonly implement cache-aside with TTLs and request coalescing

keyMetrics.throughput: Cache backend dependent
keyMetrics.latency: Cache hits often sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Cost is the chosen cache capacity

commonMistakes: No TTL
Cache stampede on popular expiry
Serving stale data after writes
components.interviewTips: Describe miss flow, stale data, invalidation, TTL jitter, negative caching, request coalescing, and why caches are not sources of truth.

components.name: Write-Through Cache
components.tagline: Writes data through the cache while persisting to the backing store
components.whatItDoes: A write-through cache updates the cache as part of the write flow and ensures the backing store is also updated. Reads are more likely to find fresh cached values, but write latency and failure handling become more complex. The implementation must define ordering and durability semantics.
whenToUse: Read-heavy data where newly written values should be immediately cached
Controlled write paths with predictable cache keys
Systems willing to pay extra write overhead for read freshness
whenNotToUse: High write volume where most values are never read
When cache failure must never block durable writes unless explicitly designed

realWorldUsage.useCase: Offer write-through integration patterns
May keep frequently read product or session state warm after updates

keyMetrics.throughput: Limited by cache and backing-store write path
keyMetrics.latency: Writes are slower than cache-aside because multiple systems participate
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Cost is cache plus backing-store usage

commonMistakes: Unclear behavior if cache succeeds but database fails
No idempotency on retry
Caching every write even when reuse is low
components.interviewTips: Compare write-through, write-behind, and cache-aside. Discuss partial failure, ordering, durability, and when a simpler invalidation strategy is safer.

components.name: Read Replica
components.tagline: Copies database data to additional nodes for reads and resilience
components.whatItDoes: A read replica receives changes from a primary database and serves read traffic. Replicas increase read capacity and can support failover, reporting, and regional locality. Replication is often asynchronous, so applications must decide when stale reads are acceptable.
whenToUse: Reporting queries separated from transactional primary
Disaster recovery and regional read locality
whenNotToUse: Read-after-write paths requiring guaranteed freshness unless routed to primary
Scaling write throughput without sharding

realWorldUsage.useCase: Operates replicated database topologies
Route selected reads to replicas to protect primaries

keyMetrics.throughput: Read capacity increases with replicas
keyMetrics.latency: Local reads may be faster; freshness depends on replication lag
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Additional database instance and storage cost per replica

commonMistakes: Sending all reads to replicas including read-after-write flows
No replication-lag monitoring
Assuming failover is automatic and lossless without testing
components.interviewTips: Explain synchronous versus asynchronous replication, lag, read-after-write consistency, failover, promotion, read routing, and that replicas do not scale writes.

components.name: Database Sharding
components.tagline: Splits data across independent database partitions
components.whatItDoes: Sharding partitions rows or documents across database nodes using a shard key. Each shard handles a subset of data, increasing write and storage capacity. The gain comes with operational complexity: cross-shard queries, rebalancing, hot partitions, and distributed transactions.
whenToUse: Write scale beyond a single database primary
Large datasets that exceed one node's practical limits
whenNotToUse: Small systems that can scale vertically or optimize queries first
Workloads dominated by cross-shard joins

realWorldUsage.useCase: Has publicly discussed sharding PostgreSQL-backed workloads
Provides built-in sharding using shard keys

keyMetrics.throughput: Can scale horizontally when load is well distributed
keyMetrics.latency: Single-shard queries remain efficient; scatter-gather queries add cost
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Multiple database nodes plus routing and operational overhead

commonMistakes: Choosing a hot shard key
No resharding strategy
Allowing uncontrolled scatter-gather queries
components.interviewTips: Discuss shard key selection, routing, rebalancing, virtual shards, hot partitions, global indexes, cross-shard transactions, and migration strategy.

components.name: Circuit Breaker
components.tagline: Stops repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency
components.whatItDoes: A circuit breaker tracks failures and temporarily blocks calls when a dependency is unhealthy. It moves through closed, open, and half-open states, allowing limited probes before normal traffic resumes. The pattern protects threads, latency budgets, and downstream recovery.
whenToUse: Protecting thread pools during partial outages
whenNotToUse: Hiding persistent errors without alerting
Using a breaker without timeouts and bounded retries

realWorldUsage.useCase: Popularized circuit-breaker patterns in microservice systems
Use breakers around external provider calls

keyMetrics.throughput: Improves effective capacity during dependency failure
keyMetrics.latency: Open-state failures return quickly rather than waiting for timeout
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Implemented in libraries, proxies, or meshes

commonMistakes: No timeout before the breaker
Same threshold for every dependency
Fallback that overloads another service
components.interviewTips: Explain states, thresholds, timeouts, retries, fallback, bulkheads, metrics, and why a breaker is not a substitute for fixing the dependency.

components.name: Saga
components.tagline: Coordinates multi-service business transactions through compensating actions
components.whatItDoes: A saga breaks a distributed business workflow into local transactions. Each successful step triggers the next step; failures cause compensating actions where possible. Sagas avoid locking resources across services but require explicit workflow state, idempotency, and business-aware recovery.
whenToUse: Orders involving payment, inventory, and shipping services
whenNotToUse: Workflows where compensation is impossible and strict atomicity is mandatory
Simple transactions inside one database

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use saga-like workflows for order processing
Coordinate reservations with compensating cancellations

keyMetrics.throughput: Workflow and broker dependent
keyMetrics.latency: Often spans seconds or longer because steps are asynchronous
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Application orchestration and messaging infrastructure

commonMistakes: Treating compensation as perfect rollback
No idempotency keys
Losing workflow state during retries
components.interviewTips: Discuss choreography versus orchestration, local transactions, compensation, idempotency, timeouts, audit history, and when 2PC is inappropriate.

components.name: CQRS
components.tagline: Separates write commands from read models
components.whatItDoes: Command Query Responsibility Segregation uses different models for writes and reads. Commands enforce business rules, while read projections are optimized for query needs. CQRS can improve scale and clarity in complex domains, but projection lag and operational complexity make it unnecessary for ordinary CRUD.
whenToUse: Different read and write scaling needs
Complex domain logic with specialized read views
Event-driven projections for dashboards or feeds
whenNotToUse: Simple CRUD applications
Teams unable to operate eventual consistency and projection rebuilds

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use read projections for fast user-facing views
May separate command validation from query models

keyMetrics.throughput: Can scale read and write paths independently
keyMetrics.latency: Read projections may lag behind writes
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Additional storage, messaging, and operational complexity

commonMistakes: Applying CQRS everywhere
No plan to rebuild projections
Hiding eventual consistency from product behavior
components.interviewTips: Explain command model, query model, projections, eventual consistency, rebuilds, event sourcing relationship, and why CQRS is optional.

components.name: Event Sourcing
components.tagline: Persists state changes as an append-only event history
components.whatItDoes: Event sourcing stores domain events rather than only the latest row state. Current state is reconstructed by replaying events or reading projections. The history supports audit and temporal analysis, but schema evolution, replay cost, and operational discipline are substantial.
whenToUse: Auditable domains where change history is a core requirement
Building projections for multiple read models
whenNotToUse: Ordinary CRUD where an audit table is enough
Teams without a plan for event versioning and replay

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use append-only ledger-like histories
Record changes that can be replayed into projections

keyMetrics.throughput: Append throughput depends on event store and partitioning
keyMetrics.latency: Writes can be efficient; projection freshness varies
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Event storage plus projection infrastructure

commonMistakes: Treating events as mutable records
Publishing internal implementation details as permanent event contracts
No snapshot or replay strategy
components.interviewTips: Discuss immutable events, projections, snapshots, schema evolution, replay, idempotency, ordering, audit benefits, and the difference from a normal event bus.

components.name: Consistent Hashing
components.tagline: Maps keys to nodes while minimizing remapping during membership changes
components.whatItDoes: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a logical ring or uses an equivalent partitioning scheme. Adding or removing a node moves only part of the keyspace instead of reshuffling everything. Virtual nodes improve balance and make capacity adjustments smoother.
whenToUse: Routing keys across changing worker fleets
whenNotToUse: Small static clusters where modulo hashing is sufficient
Ignoring replication and hot-key behavior

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses partitioning concepts to distribute data
Partitions keys across hash slots for cluster routing

keyMetrics.throughput: Routing is local and inexpensive
keyMetrics.latency: Minimal computation overhead
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Algorithmic pattern; no direct service charge

commonMistakes: Too few virtual nodes
No replication strategy
Assuming balanced key counts means balanced workload
components.interviewTips: Explain modulo-hash remapping problem, ring, virtual nodes, replication, hotspots, rebalancing, and why many systems use slots or tokens.

components.name: Bloom Filter
components.tagline: Probabilistic membership check that trades false positives for compact memory use
components.whatItDoes: A Bloom filter answers whether an item may be present or is definitely absent. It uses multiple hash functions over a bit array. False positives are possible, but false negatives are not expected when the structure is used correctly and items are not removed without a compatible variant.
whenNotToUse: Needing an authoritative membership answer
Supporting deletion without a counting or compatible variant

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses Bloom-filter-style techniques to avoid unnecessary storage reads
Use probabilistic structures for compact membership checks

keyMetrics.throughput: Very high in-memory lookup throughput
keyMetrics.latency: Typically microseconds or less
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Memory cost determined by item count and desired false-positive rate

commonMistakes: Treating a positive result as proof
Sizing without expected cardinality
Using a normal Bloom filter when deletion is required
components.interviewTips: Explain bit array, hash functions, false positives, no false negatives under normal assumptions, sizing, and practical database-read avoidance.

components.name: Two-Phase Commit
components.tagline: Coordinates atomic commit across multiple participants
components.whatItDoes: Two-phase commit asks participants to prepare, then instructs them to commit or abort. It can provide atomicity across resources but introduces coordinator dependency, blocking risk, and latency. Modern distributed application designs often prefer local transactions plus sagas unless strict atomicity is essential.
whenToUse: Database systems with built-in distributed transaction support
Rare workflows where partial completion is unacceptable
whenNotToUse: Long-running internet-scale workflows
Microservice processes where availability matters more than immediate atomicity

realWorldUsage.useCase: Support prepared transactions or distributed commit protocols
Coordinate multiple transactional resources

keyMetrics.throughput: Lower than local transactions due to coordination
keyMetrics.latency: At least multiple network rounds plus participant work
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Operational complexity and reduced availability during failures

commonMistakes: Using 2PC casually across unreliable services
No coordinator recovery plan
Holding locks for long periods
components.interviewTips: Explain prepare and commit phases, coordinator failure, blocking, lock duration, availability trade-offs, and when saga-based compensation is more suitable.

components.name: Prometheus
components.tagline: Pull-based metrics collection and alerting toolkit
components.whatItDoes: Prometheus scrapes numeric time-series metrics from targets and stores samples with labels. PromQL queries power dashboards and alerts. It is strong for operational monitoring, but cardinality must be controlled and long-term retention often needs additional architecture.
whenToUse: SLO alerting based on latency, errors, traffic, and saturation
whenNotToUse: Storing arbitrary high-cardinality event logs
Using labels for user IDs or request IDs

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses Prometheus extensively for cloud-native monitoring
Commonly pair Prometheus metrics with Grafana dashboards

keyMetrics.throughput: Depends on scrape interval, target count, and cardinality
keyMetrics.latency: Near-real-time scrape and query behavior
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Open-source software; storage and managed-service cost vary

commonMistakes: High-cardinality labels
No retention plan
Alerts based only on internal causes rather than user symptoms
components.interviewTips: Discuss metrics model, labels, scraping, PromQL, alerting rules, service discovery, cardinality, federation or remote write, and SLO-oriented alerts.

components.name: Grafana
components.tagline: Dashboard and visualization layer for operational data
components.whatItDoes: Grafana queries data sources such as Prometheus, logs, traces, and databases, then presents dashboards and alerts. It helps teams correlate system behavior visually. A dashboard is only useful when panels answer operational questions rather than display every available metric.
whenNotToUse: Replacing durable telemetry storage
Creating dozens of panels with no clear action

realWorldUsage.useCase: Used broadly for monitoring dashboards
Pair Grafana with Prometheus and log backends

keyMetrics.throughput: Depends on dashboard query load and data sources
keyMetrics.latency: Interactive query latency should usually remain seconds or less
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Open source or managed plans; cost varies

commonMistakes: Dashboard overload
No variables or drill-down paths
Using averages that hide tail latency
components.interviewTips: Discuss data sources, panels, variables, alerting, p95/p99 latency, dashboard ownership, and the difference between visualization and telemetry storage.

components.name: Jaeger
components.tagline: Distributed tracing system for following requests across services
components.whatItDoes: Jaeger collects spans that describe how a request moves through distributed services. Trace context connects parent and child operations, making latency bottlenecks and failure paths visible. Sampling is important because recording every trace can be expensive.
whenNotToUse: Replacing metrics for aggregate health
Collecting every trace at high volume without cost planning

realWorldUsage.useCase: Uses Jaeger-compatible tracing for distributed systems
Export traces to Jaeger and other tracing backends

keyMetrics.throughput: Collector capacity depends on span volume and sampling
keyMetrics.latency: Trace ingestion is asynchronous; query latency varies
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Open-source software; storage and collector cost vary

commonMistakes: No propagation of trace IDs across async boundaries
Sampling only successful requests
Adding huge payloads as span attributes
components.interviewTips: Explain traces, spans, context propagation, sampling, baggage, async messaging, tail latency, and how tracing complements metrics and logs.

components.name: ELK Stack
components.tagline: Searchable centralized logs using Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana
components.whatItDoes: The ELK pattern centralizes logs so teams can search incidents across hosts and services. Elasticsearch indexes log documents, Logstash or alternative agents transform and ship records, and Kibana visualizes queries. Structured logs, retention, and index lifecycle controls are essential for cost and usability.
whenNotToUse: Using verbose logs as a substitute for metrics and traces
Keeping unlimited logs without retention controls

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use Elastic Stack for observability and security analytics
Centralize structured logs for incident response

keyMetrics.throughput: Depends on ingest volume, shard design, and retention
keyMetrics.latency: Search often targets seconds or less for recent logs
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Storage and compute can become substantial at high ingest volumes

commonMistakes: Unstructured free-text-only logs
Logging secrets or personal data unnecessarily
Too many shards and no lifecycle policy
components.interviewTips: Discuss structured logging, correlation IDs, index lifecycle, retention, redaction, shard sizing, search costs, and why logs are one observability signal.

components.name: PagerDuty
components.tagline: On-call alert routing and incident-response coordination platform
components.whatItDoes: PagerDuty receives alerts, applies routing and escalation policies, and notifies the responsible responders. It helps organize on-call rotations and incident workflows. The platform cannot compensate for noisy alerts; teams must alert on actionable user-impacting symptoms.
whenToUse: Routing production alerts to on-call engineers
Coordinating incident response and post-incident follow-up
whenNotToUse: Sending every warning to a human
Using paging as a substitute for automated recovery

realWorldUsage.useCase: Use on-call platforms for escalation and incident response
Emphasizes timely, actionable, symptom-based alerts

keyMetrics.throughput: Alert volume should be deliberately low and actionable
keyMetrics.latency: Notifications should arrive within minutes for urgent incidents
keyMetrics.typicalCost: Usually per-user subscription pricing

commonMistakes: Alert fatigue
No clear service ownership
Paging on causes that do not affect users
components.interviewTips: Discuss severity, escalation policies, on-call ownership, actionable alerts, deduplication, runbooks, incident roles, and blameless postmortems.
